Transliterated as tijeep, it has same tone as trill of Primary Song. In 3 observed instances, given with wing raise (see Behavior: Agonistic Behavior), just before or after copulation (169)"
NC.notes:
found the paper with the original finding https://www.jstor.org/stable/pdf/4084602.pdf -- 3 instances of females producing a songlike vocalization out of ~20 pairs observed, feels like it is relatively common?
  "Female songlike vocalization. This sounds to the human ear as a "tijeeep" or "beeert," buzzy and with the same tone as the trill of the primary song. This sound was heard from only three females, just before or immediately after copulation. It is given with the wing raise, either from the ground or an elevated perch. The female songlike vocalization attracts males, and it may serve a function similar to the whinny. The sound is called songlike because of its resemblance to the primary song, and because it appears to serve a more narrow function than the whinny, that of attracting a mate to the female's vicinity."
NC.assessment: present? ~3/20 feels common enough to say present?

BOW.Quote: Helpers may aid the breeding pair in raising young (Brackbill 1970b, Tarbell 1983). At one nest, the helper was one of the previous year's offspring of the adult female and a different male (Brackbill 1970b). In another case, the helper was the offspring of the breeding pair from a previous season (Tarbell 1983). Such helping behavior is unusual for parids and has only been reported in two other species, Bridled Titmice (Baeolophus wollweberi; Nocedal and Ficken 1998a) and Black Tits (Parus niger; Brown 1987). There is no information on whether helping affects breeding success of the adult pair.

"Males in their first breeding season, still wearing drab brownish female-like garb from their first Prebasic molt, sing much like older males, giving the false impression that both sexes sing with equal complexity... BOW.Quote: At four nests in New York, more than two adult Bobolinks fed nestlings (Beason and Trout 1984, Bollinger et al. 1986). Two instances of this phenomenon involving multiple adults in Wisconsin (Martin 1971b). Electrophoretic analyses of adults and nestlings at nest in New York indicated possibility that both feeding males may have sired nestlings or that one male may have been previous year's offspring of one or both of other adults (Bollinger et al. 1986). SGM recorded feeding schedule data at nest with young fed by two Bobolinks and a female Eastern Meadowlark that had lost her brood to predator.

Common.name: redthroated ant-tanagers
BOW.Quote: Females only incubate and brood the young, but both males and females bring food to the nestlings. Group members help during nesting. During nest building, group members only follow the nest building female around the territory, although Willis (1961) observed one non-reproductive individual carrying material to the nest. Helpers contribute with nest defense and feeding nestlings; helpers start feeding nestlings on day 5 after hatching and, on average, they make 4.5% (18 of the 397) of the total feeding trips (Willis 1961).

BOW.Quote: Nests often attract the attention of extra adults that associate with a pair for up to an entire breeding season; these extra birds are sometimes tolerated and occasionally lead to polygyny (217). In New York, extra birds were predominantly males (219, 325), whereas in Washington, extra birds were yearling females (217). Extra adults contribute relatively little to feeding young, but they are known to mob predators and assist in nest-building, incubation, and brooding young (219, 325, 217). Extra adults may be using nest attendance as a breeding strategy either to replace one pair member should something happen to it (217) or to commit sexually selected infanticide (219, 325), providing an opportunity for males to take over the breeding female (see Behavior: Sexual Behavior). Nests that are attended by helpers often are ones occupied by older females (325), consistent with the interpretation that male attendants are trying to secure high-quality females as mates.

Social_breeding_system_when_cooperative: pair nesting with related male and female helpers; widespread conspecific brood parasitism
BOW.Quote: essentially monogamous, most pairs staying together for life, taking on helpers in some years or themselves helping to rear close relatives’ young in others; during its lifetime, individual can change roles between breeding and helping several times; colonies  generally of 10–20 nests attended by 30–80 birds, some of up to 450 birds; 60% of breeding pairs have 1–5 helpers, these being yearlings or experienced past breeders, which help with excavation, incubation, brood-feeding, and defence of nest and feeding territory; 3–4 pairs with helpers comprise a clan, members of which are related and freely visit each other’s burrows, but repel attempts by non-members to enter burrows; 2 populations studied at Nakuru, Kenya, comprised c. 400 birds in 60 clans at 100 active nests; males preponderate, and most helpers are male

BOW.Quote: Although ca. 20% of Canada Jay pairs studied in Quebec and Ontario have an associated nonbreeder on their territories at the onset of breeding and ca. 65% of these are the pair's own offspring from the previous breeding season, the nonbreeders do not feed the current year's nestlings and the breeders energetically drive them away if they approach the nest. Starting immediately after the nestlings fledge, however, adults relax this vigilance and on intensively observed territories in Ontario and Quebec some non-breeders have accounted for over 30% of all observed feedings of the young (189, 190). Proposed explanation for this pattern holds that, compared to other jays, Canada Jays are particularly vulnerable to nest predators because they have poorer defensive abilities (being smaller and generally having only one extra group member, if any). In such a species, suppression of allofeeding, along with a smaller than expected clutch size and a very low provisioning rate by the adults (achieved by bringing largest possible loads at the consequently minimum possible frequency), may reduce predator-attracting visits to the nest and thus contribute to higher breeding success (166, 191). Strickland, D. and T. A. Waite. (2001). Does initial suppression of allofeeding in small jays help to conceal their nests? Canadian Journal of Zoology 79 (12):2128-2146. Strickland, D. (2003). Ontario Gray Jays help on the world stage: Part 2. Ontario Birds 21 (1):15-22.

Other_FemaleSong: "Babble-Singing, Soft Singing, Whisper Song, and Rhythmic Singing. Often accompanied by raised head and flashing of white nictitating membrane; usually uttered only by males. Probably the equivalent of song in other passerines; can be heard from only about 50 m (Baeyens 1979a). Dominant Black-billed Magpies often approach predator, or even human intruder, and challenge it by Babble-Singing in self-assertive manner; described as ‚Äúcheeky‚Äù behavior by Birkhead (Birkhead 1991), when directed toward him. Often starts with soft chatters of 1 or 2 notes; then gradually progresses into whistled subsong of 6‚Äì7 syllables. For a sonogram of this and several other calls, see Birkhead 1991: 68. This challenging or assertive behavior given around predators has never been observed in European magpies (Birkhead 1991). Soft Singing is uttered quietly, usually by courting males; similar Whisper Song is given by both sexes during nest-building (Cramp and Perrins 1994a). Louder Rhythmic Singing also given by males during courtship. Both Soft Singing and Rhythmic Singing sound like subsongs. Rhythmic Singing seems more rigid in sequence and stereotyped than Babble-Singing. Babble-Singing is often given by young, aggressive males, but a wild adult female was heard to give this varied whistlelike song while sitting alone in a flight cage (CHT), and young magpies between 6 and 20 wk old have been heard uttering this call (Cramp and Perrins 1994a). "

"The purpose of this note is to add two species, the Indigo Bunting (Passerina cyanea) and the Rufous-sided Towhee (Pipilo erythrophthalmus) , to the list of those in which the females, ‚Äúordinarily considered songless, may occasionally sing‚Äù (M. M. Nice. 1943. Trans. Linnaean SOC. New York, 6:131). Both bunting and towhee were heard near Bloomington, Indiana, on dates falling at the very beginnings of the nesting seasons of their respective species in this locality... Pipilo erythrophthalnuu-At 4:30 a.m. on April 23, 1957, a cloudy morning with the
 temperature at 65‚Äù, I heard a loud and unfamiliar song, faintly reminiscent of the utterance of the male towhee. A female was perched 14 feet high in the top of a flowering
 dogwood (Cornas florida) in an old field; in five minutes she sang 15 times, then flew
 down and fell silent. I heard her no more, although I passed the spot daily and in June
 spent two full days watching warbler nests nearby. A male towhee held territory there,
 but he was not in evidence within 15 minutes of the time when the female sang"; "Female Song. Reported by Nolan (Nolan 1958b) from Indiana and observed once by JSG (9 May 1971, New York). Indiana female was mated; she sang an ‚Äúunmusical, flat, somewhat squeaky‚Äù song at rate of about 1 song/20 s over 5-min period. New York female sang 2 weak, husky, flat shreeeeee trills from high perches and then flew, followed by her mate, who was nearby."

Song transliterated as oiksee-oiksee, but otherwise undescribed; song was similar to group of 2-syllable songs sung by males in same population (9). Roberts (13) reported female song in P. m. oregonus that resembled quiet singing by male. It was muted, continuous, variable, musical, and without apparent temporal organization; it included as elements Mew Call, Lisp Call, Growl, ‚Äú Tsk ‚Äù note, brief Whinny, two different trills, and slow, metallic warbling. Female sang quiet song while foraging and moving about on ground, while male sang above her (28 Jun)."

BOW.Quote: In contrast to Western Bluebirds, Eastern Bluebirds rarely have helpers. In joint nesting, 2 females lay 2 clutches of eggs synchronously in the same nest, then incubate synchronously and sequentially, and cooperate with a male in feeding nestlings and fledglings. In S. Carolina, 5 of 4,299 nesting attempts in field seasons 1977–1991 were joint nesting ventures; 2 of these 5 attempts were by the same previously known and banded females, so it was reliably inferred that these jointly-nesting females were mother and daughter (PAG, JHP). Juvenile helpers are rare; almost all reports are of juveniles entering nesting cavities when adults are feeding later broods (Pinkowski 1975d)—something documented on video films twice by PAG and JHP. Adult helpers seen occasionally and irregularly (Pinkowski 1976d, PAG), usually second-year son of current breeders.

Other_FemaleSong: Vocal; calls all year, mainly in austral spring. Male song varied, 5–10 ringing whistles, first two usually short and higher-pitched; can be slow and measured "hi-hhh-hay-kway-kway-kway-kway-kway-kway" or faster "pikwik-koi-koi-koi-koi-koi-koi" or almost trilled "wikokokokokoko"; either ascending "ki-ki-ki-ki-heeee" (very like song of C. sulfureopectus) or descending, slowing "hi-hi-tew-tew-tiew-tiew-teyouw"; males often counter-sing with each other, using same calls. Female occasionally joins in with a few tearing scolds, "zzrrreee-zzrrreee".

Other_FemaleSong: "Song of presumed male, from within upper canopy of prominent tree or from near top of thick bush, variable, ventriloquial, of pure ringing whistles, 3 or 4 short notes and one long one, "wi-hi-hi-hi-wheeee", first note sometimes lower ("woo-hi-hi-heeee"), the whole sometimes descending, as "hi-hi-hu-hu-hu-yooo"; a second common song is faster, with 4–9 (up to 15) notes on one pitch, 5 notes per second, "wi-wi-wi-wi-wi-wi-wi", and even faster versions higher-pitched. Some geographical variation: in Sene­gal typically a 4-note "put-wit-too-weee" and 2-note "hoop, heeee", each repeated in series; in Ivory Coast mainly a 3-note "hooey-hooey-hooey", also repeated in series. Presumed female sometimes responds with quiet, husky "skizzz" or "tzzrrik-tzzrrik". "

Common.name: house wren
BOW.Quote: Extremely rare if not absent in most temperate populations. One report from California of a juvenile from a first brood helping its father (and possibly mother; she was unmarked) feed young of a second brood in the same season (275. Second report from Kansas of a juvenile of unknown origin feeding young and removing a fecal sac from a nest at least one time (Timson and Farley 2003). Helpers-at-the-nest also reported in Costa Rica, but not in all nests and such behavior was apparently rare (Skutch 1940, 176, Skutch 1983, Winnett-Murray 1986). Skutch (1983) speculated helping was more likely when young from a previous brood sleep with the mother in the nest while she incubates in a subsequent breeding attempt. In one case in Costa Rica, an individual known not to be the offspring of a resident parents' previous brood attempted to feed young; parents repeatedly attacked that individual (Winnett-Murray 1986: 23).

Common.name: eastern kingbird
BOW.Quote: Does not occur (17, MTM). Trios of adults occasionally form, but are rarely stable; a trio in New York remained together from early in nestling period to > 1 mo after young had fledged (MTM). The fate of the third bird in next year was determined in 2 of 3 cases in which the third bird was banded and sex determined. In one case, a female returned to breed on territory where she was seen in previous year (former male and female occupants of territory failed to return). In the other case, a male established residence on adjacent territory in following year. Third birds in trios probably represent birds prospecting for a breeding site in the next year. One case of incest is known: an experienced female (> 9 yr old) bred with a son raised in previous year (MTM).  Smith, W. J. (1966d). Communication and relationships in the genus Tyrannus. Publications of the Nuttall Ornithological Club 6:1-250.
